strengths: One-call opening (`tracker_review_queue`) removes all decision-making from the first minute of a session; the tutor never has to ask her what to do. Keep it.

The 'skipping habit' script ('what's one thing you could write down?') has demonstrably worked: blanks went from 27 of 39 marks lost on Paper 3F (Jul 2026) to zero on the 19 Aug exit check and zero on 2 Sep. Do not remove the line; extend it (finding 10).

'Never hand over the answer first', 'one hint at a time', 'model solutions only after her genuine attempt' and 'mistakes are information' are exactly the right stance for a student whose failure mode is avoidance rather than ignorance.

The exit ticket is independent and the promotion rules are conservative (never two levels, never on one question, taught-and-tested-same-day = developing). That protects her from a dashboard that lies, which is what keeps a progress chart motivating.

Session summaries are unusually honest and specific: they recorded 'answers submitted without working', 'Q4 and Q5 not submitted before the session ended', the answer-targeting slip and the prose-not-boxes habit. The raw material for every finding below already exists in the log; the skill just has no rule that acts on it.
'Planned next' resumes exactly where she stopped ('Resume at practice Q4'), so unfinished work is not lost. Finding 4 only asks that this be said to her as well as written to the tracker.
Foundation-before-Higher ordering and the formula-sheet rule ('practise selecting formulas, not reciting them') are correct GCSE technique and reduce the memorisation load.
The frustration line already signposts the parent for anything beyond normal study frustration, and the tone rule 'no walls of text' is right for chat; finding 12 makes it operational.
The parent's no-streaks stance is consistent with everything in this lens: nothing proposed below introduces streaks, badges or obligation; the additions are structure, timing and closure.

findings.title: Shape A is 80-90 unbroken minutes with no break, no chunk boundary and no daily cap
findings.where: maths-tutor-session/SKILL.md lines 53-58, section 'Session shapes', Shape A
findings.problem: Current text: "**A. Full session (~90 min learning block)** ... 1. **Starter (10 min)** ... 2. **Teach (30–40 min)** ... 3. **Practise (30 min):** 5–8 questions ... 4. **Exit ticket (10 min)** ... 5. **Log to the tracker**". That is 10 + 30-40 + 30 + 10 = 80-90 continuous minutes, the longest single block (Teach) is 30-40 minutes of largely tutor-led explanation, and there is no break anywhere. Nothing limits how many Shape A sessions run in a day. On 2 Sep two ran back to back. The first (session 2) went starter 5/5, exit ticket 4/4, zero issues. The second (session 3) produced the day's only wrong starter answer (A4, which triggered a demotion), both answer-only submissions, the answer-targeting slip on Q3, two of five practice questions never submitted, and no exit ticket was logged at all (practice runs 12 and 13 only).
findings.why_it_matters: Sustained attention and vigilance decline over time is the core ADHD deficit, and it is steeper in the afternoon and in a second block of the same task. A 13-year-old with ADHD asked to hold 90 minutes of maths in chat with no break will produce exactly the pattern in the 2 Sep log: accuracy holds early, then working disappears, then questions go unfinished. Every one of those late-session slips was then recorded as evidence about her maths (A4 demoted) when at least part of it is evidence about session design.
findings.proposal:
Replace Shape A with: "**A. Full session (~90 min, two halves with a break)** — 'what should I do today', new topic work. Tell her the shape and the times before the first question; she cannot see a clock in chat, so you are it.
0. **Open (2 min):** see 'Opening and closing'.
1. **Starter (10 min):** 5 retrieval questions filled by the 'Starter spacing' schedule. One calculator mode for the whole starter, said once. Mark together.
2. **Teach (20 min, +10 only if she is still with you):** the top priority gap from the review queue unless she names a topic. One example you lead, one she leads, then check in: 'still good, or break now?'
— **Break (5 min, mandatory):** say it, don't offer it. Away from the screen. Agree a return time. Restart with one easy question on today's topic, not a recap speech.
3. **Practise (25 min):** 4–6 questions, easy → exam-style, one per message. Stop when the time is up, not when the set is finished; an unfinished question is logged, not pushed through.
4. **Exit ticket (10 min):** 4 fresh questions on today's topic, independent, then marked. 3–4 correct = topic moves toward 🟡/🟢.
5. **Close (3 min):** see 'Opening and closing'.
6. **Log to the tracker** (below).

**Daily load: one Shape A per day.** If she asks for more the same day, offer Shape B or a 20-minute practice-only block on today's topic and say why: a second full session in one day is where working stops being shown and questions stop being finished. Two Shape A sessions on one day is not a reason to run a shorter session tomorrow — it is a reason not to run the second one."
findings.evidence_needed: Vigilance decrement / time-on-task decline in adolescents with ADHD, and effect of scheduled breaks on on-task behaviour and accuracy (ADHD-direct); guideline support for environmental modification such as breaks (NICE NG87 or equivalent).

findings.title: No protocol for an answer submitted without working, so the path of least resistance in chat wins
findings.where: maths-tutor-session/SKILL.md line 68, section 'Teaching rules — non-negotiable', first bullet; and line 71 'Exam working'
findings.problem: Current text: "**Never hand over the answer first.** Ask what she'd try; give one hint at a time; let her do the working. Model solutions only after her genuine attempt." and "**Exam working:** steps shown, substitutions written, units stated, answers underlined." The rules say working must be shown; nothing says what the tutor does when it isn't. Session 3 log: "Answers were submitted without working despite working being requested on two questions"; A17 "answer only with no working, despite working being asked for"; session 2: "division line 45 ÷ 0.8 not written down", "y = 3x − 4 was not written down first", and "she reports the arithmetic in prose rather than writing numbers into the tree boxes... the fill-in widget has been masking that". The tutor is marking answer-only responses as correct (starter run 12 shows 4 first-time correct) and then asking for working in general, which she ignores.
findings.why_it_matters: Impulsive responding — answer first, skip the intermediate step — is a response-inhibition problem, not a knowledge problem, and a general instruction ('show your working') does not fix it; a specific, immediate, small demand does. In the AQA exam a bare wrong answer scores 0 where a line of working would score M1; the A4 sign error (4x−7 for 4x−23) is exactly the kind of slip that method marks rescue. Typing working into chat is tedious for a 13-year-old, so the medium is pushing her toward the habit that costs marks.
findings.proposal: Add a bullet after 'Never hand over the answer first': "**An answer without working is not finished.** On any question worth 2+ marks, don't mark a bare answer — right or wrong — and don't re-ask for 'working' in general. Ask for one specific line: 'what did you do to the 7?', 'write the four terms before you collect them', 'which number went in the top-left box?'. Mark it once that line is there. Say once per session, not per question, that a bare wrong answer scores 0 and the same wrong answer with the method scores M1. Working lives on paper: a photo, or a three-line transcription, is fine; a fill-in widget that hides the working is not — use widgets for diagrams she draws into, not for answers. Algebra starter questions are always working-required." Also add to the logging section: "Record in the summary how many questions came with working out of how many that needed it (e.g. 'working shown 3/5'), so the habit is visible across sessions."
findings.evidence_needed: Response inhibition / impulsivity in ADHD and the effect of immediate, specific prompts versus general instructions (ADHD-direct); AQA 8300 mark-scheme convention that method marks are awarded for working (policy document).

findings.title: No opening for the student: she gets a retrieval question, not a plan, a time or a reason
findings.where: maths-tutor-session/SKILL.md lines 49-54, section 'Session shapes' ('Pick based on what she asks; confirm in one line, don't interrogate') through Shape A step 1
findings.problem: Current text: "Pick based on what she asks; confirm in one line, don't interrogate." then "**Starter (10 min):** 5 retrieval questions — 3 from the ageing 🟢 topics the review queue named, 2 from 🟡 topics." The first thing she experiences is a question from a topic she has not seen for 8+ weeks, with no agenda, no time budget, no mention of what was planned last time, and no easy first win. Everything in the opening is tutor-facing (the review-queue call); nothing is student-facing.
findings.why_it_matters: Task initiation is one of the executive functions most impaired in ADHD; the cost of starting is highest when the task is open-ended and the first step is hard. A visible plan with times, a reminder of last time's win and a first question she will get reduce that cost. Opening on an ageing topic she may have forgotten is opening on the question most likely to go wrong.
findings.proposal:
Add a section 'Opening and closing' after 'Session shapes', beginning: "### Opening (first two minutes)
Before the first question, in one short message:
1. The plan with times: 'Today: 10-min starter, 20 min on expected frequency, 5-min break, 25 min practice, exit ticket. Done by about [time].'
2. One thing from last session she got right, named with its number (take it from the last summary: 'your garage exit ticket was 4/4, every fraction simplified').
3. What we said we'd pick up — read the tracker's planned-next to her — so unfinished work is resumed by agreement, not sprung on her.
4. 'Energy 1–5?' — one number, no discussion. 1–2: run the 45-minute shape (starter + practice on a known topic, no new teaching) and say so. Write the number in the summary.
Then the first starter question is a warm-up she will get: one from a 🟢 topic that is not ageing. The ageing checks come second and third, never first."
findings.evidence_needed: Task-initiation / activation deficits in ADHD and the effect of advance organisers or visible schedules on engagement (ADHD-direct or guideline); testing-effect literature on beginning with an easy retrieval item (general).

findings.title: No closure, and no rule for a session that runs out of time mid-practice
findings.where: maths-tutor-session/SKILL.md lines 57-58 (Exit ticket, Log) and line 103 ('Then tell her: logged — you can see it at ...')
findings.problem: Current text ends the session with: "4. **Exit ticket (10 min):** 4 fresh questions ... 5. **Log to the tracker** (below)." and "Then tell her: *\"logged — you can see it at https://education.rmmann.co.uk/s/maths\"*." She leaves with a URL. She is not asked what she learned, is not told the specific win, and the next_steps line is written to the tracker, not said to her. There is no rule for the case that actually happened on 2 Sep: "Q4 and Q5 were not submitted before the session ended" — no exit ticket, no close, the summary says the session simply ended.
findings.why_it_matters: A session that ends on an unfinished question and no acknowledgement is a session that ends on failure, for a student whose historic pattern is avoidance. A 60-second closure where she says one thing she can now do is cheap retrieval practice and the last thing she remembers about maths that day. The early-stop rule matters because the alternative — 'just finish these two' — is what turns a tired end into a wrong answer that gets logged as evidence.
findings.proposal:
Continue the 'Opening and closing' section: "### Closing (last three minutes) — even when time ran out
1. One line from her: 'what can you do now that you couldn't at the start?' Her words, not yours.
2. One specific win with its number ('exit ticket 4/4, all simplified'). Not a list.
3. What's next, in one sentence — the same sentence you log as next_steps.
4. Log, then the 'logged — you can see it' line.

**If the clock runs out mid-block:** stop at the end of the current question, never mid-question, and never ask her to 'just finish these two'. Drop the exit ticket rather than compress it; the topic stays where it is and the summary says 'exit ticket not reached'. Name the questions not attempted and put 'resume at Qn' first in next_steps. Still do the three-line close."
findings.evidence_needed: End-of-lesson retrieval / self-explanation effect on retention (general, meta-analysis); ADHD literature on ending tasks at success to reduce task aversion (ADHD-direct or expert).

findings.title: Time exists for the tutor but never for the student; no marks-per-minute pacing
findings.where: maths-tutor-session/SKILL.md lines 53-57 (the minute figures in Shape A) and line 62 (Shape C '~45 min')
findings.problem: The only timing in the skill is the tutor-facing minute budget per block. Nothing says the times are told to her, nothing asks anyone to run a timer, nothing links marks to minutes, and the chat interface has no clock. `tracker_log_session` has no duration field (see references/tracker-service.md line 60: `subject, summary, date?, next_steps?, updates[]`), so how long a session actually took is never recorded — the 90 minutes is an assumption nobody has checked.
findings.why_it_matters: Time blindness — poor estimation of elapsed time and of how long a task will take — is well documented in ADHD, and external timers are the standard accommodation. It is also exam technique: the AQA paper gives 90 minutes for 80 marks, roughly a mark a minute, and her Paper 3F back-of-paper blanks were described in the appendix as 'a pace and confidence problem as often as a knowledge one'. She has never been taught the pace.
findings.proposal: Add to 'Teaching rules': "**Time is said out loud.** Every block starts with its minutes; every exam-style question carries its marks and rough time ('3 marks — about 3 minutes in the exam; the paper gives roughly a mark a minute'). Ask her, or her parent, to set a timer for each block. After the exit ticket ask 'how long did that take?' and write the answer in the summary. The summary's first line is always: 'Shape A · started ~HH:MM · ~N min · energy N/5 · ended by plan | by clock'." No schema change is needed for that first line; a `duration_minutes` field on `tracker_log_session` would be the M-effort follow-up.
findings.evidence_needed: Time perception / time reproduction deficits in ADHD and the effect of external timers (ADHD-direct, meta-analysis exists); AQA 8300 paper timing 90 min / 80 marks (policy document).

findings.title: Starter spacing has two buckets and misses the 3-8 week window where exam-ready evidence would come from
findings.where: maths-tutor-session/SKILL.md line 54, Shape A step 1; and gcse-progress-tracker/SKILL.md lines 74-76 (examready rule)
findings.problem: Current text: "5 retrieval questions — 3 from the ageing 🟢 topics the review queue named, 2 from 🟡 topics." The only spacing intervals are 'ageing' (secure, untouched 8+ weeks) and 'developing'. The examready rule needs "a spaced re-test ≥3 weeks after going secure", but a topic secured 3–8 weeks ago is neither ageing nor developing, so the schedule never samples it: A17 was retested at 20 days only because a planned-next note named it, and was then not promotable because it was a single question one day short. There is also no 1-session interval (yesterday's topic) and no 'until three clean' rule for a demoted or wobbling topic: A4 slipped on the same sub-skill on 16 Aug, 19 Aug and 2 Sep and was still only in the starter by chance.
findings.why_it_matters: Spacing and retrieval practice are the two best-evidenced learning effects, and expanding intervals (1 session, ~1 week, ~3 weeks, 8+ weeks) is how a topic actually reaches and holds 'examready'. With 12 of the 16 secure topics currently outside the ageing window, most of her secure work is invisible to the starter. For a student with ADHD the starter also has to be the place where a shaky sub-skill is rehearsed little and often rather than retaught in a 40-minute block.
findings.proposal:
Replace step 1 with: "**Starter (10 min):** 5 questions, one per message, filled in this order; if a slot has no candidate give it to the next one down:
1. **Warm-up** — a 🟢 topic that is not ageing and not on watch. A win to start.
2. **Last session's topic** (1-session spacing).
3. **A watch loose end or a topic demoted in the last fortnight.** It returns every session until it has three clean answers in a row, working shown, then drops to slot 4.
4. **A 🟢 topic secured 3–8 weeks ago** (last-touched from `tracker_get_state`) — the exam-ready re-test window; nothing else samples it. Two clean answers across two sessions in this window, working shown, is the evidence `gcse-progress-tracker` needs.
5. **An ageing 🟢** (8+ weeks) from the review queue.
🟡 topics not touched this fortnight take any slot that falls through." Follow-up (M, service side): have `tracker_review_queue` return a fourth group, 'due exam-ready re-test (secure 3–8 weeks)', so the skill does not have to compute it from last-touched dates.
findings.evidence_needed: Spacing effect and expanding-interval retrieval in mathematics (meta-analysis, general population); retrieval practice benefit in students with ADHD or learning difficulties (ADHD-direct if available).

findings.title: Exam technique is implicit; the reading-the-question error that keeps recurring is never taught as a skill
findings.where: maths-tutor-session/SKILL.md lines 71-72 ('Exam working', 'Formula sheet') and line 62 (Shape C weekly check)
findings.problem: Current text: "**Exam working:** steps shown, substitutions written, units stated, answers underlined. Explain marks as an AQA examiner would (M/A/B)." That is presentation of an answer. Nothing covers reading the question: the log calls answer-targeting 'the recurring answer-targeting habit' (all three colours when only blues were asked), and both Q2(b) and Q3(b) on 2 Sep were left unsimplified when Q3(b) asked for simplest form — 'that would have lost an A mark'. The Weekly check (Shape C) is 'exam-style mixed questions' with no timing and no move-on rule, so it does not rehearse the pace problem that produced the Paper 3F blanks.
findings.why_it_matters: For a student with ADHD, misreading what is asked is a predictable attention error, not carelessness, and it is trainable with a fixed two-second routine. Every mark it saves is a mark she already knows how to earn. A timed weekly check with a move-on rule is the only place the 'write one line and come back' habit gets rehearsed under the conditions where it failed.
findings.proposal: Add two bullets after 'Exam working': "**Read-the-question routine on every exam-style question:** before any maths she types (a) what is being asked for, in her words, and (b) the marks. Two words is enough: 'blues only, 2 marks' / 'simplest form, 3 marks'. Answer-targeting and unsimplified 'simplest form' answers are reading errors, not maths errors, and this is the fix. Keep it until she has done it unprompted for a fortnight, then drop the prompt and watch." and "**The weekly check (C) is timed** at a mark a minute with a visible timer, and she is told the rule once: 90 seconds stuck → write one line, move on, come back at the end. Report blanks and questions-returned-to in the summary."
findings.evidence_needed: Test-wiseness / exam-technique instruction effect on scores (general, review); attention-related reading errors in ADHD and the value of fixed routines or checklists (ADHD-direct or expert).

findings.title: The skill never asks about energy or time of day, and should — but must not ask her about medication or sleep
findings.where: maths-tutor-session/SKILL.md whole file (no occurrence of energy, time, morning, afternoon, sleep or medication); gcse-progress-tracker/references/subjects/maths.md (no session-window line)
findings.problem: Nothing in either skill or the appendix mentions time of day, energy, sleep or medication, and no field records when a session started. The brief says nothing is known about medication. On 2 Sep two full sessions ran on one day and the second degraded; the log cannot say whether it was late afternoon, and nothing would have stopped it.
findings.why_it_matters: If she is on stimulant medication its coverage window is the single biggest predictor of a good session; if she is not, time of day and sleep still are, and sleep problems are common in adolescents with ADHD. But an AI tutor asking a 13-year-old about her medication every session is intrusive, is the parent's domain, and would make the session feel clinical. The right split is: one non-medical number from her, one line of configuration from the parent, and a timestamp in the log so the pattern can be seen later.
findings.proposal: 1) In the Opening (finding 3) keep 'Energy 1–5?' as the only question to her; never ask about medication, sleep or meals. 2) Add to maths.md under a new heading '## Session window (parent-maintained)': "Best window for a full session: [parent fills, e.g. 09:30–13:00]. Avoid: [e.g. after 16:00]. Maximum one Shape A per day. The tutor reads this at open; if asked to run Shape A outside the window it says so in one line and offers the 45-minute shape instead." The parent adds anything medication-related here in their own words, or not at all. 3) Add to the tutor skill's logging rules: "The summary's first line carries start time, approximate duration, energy 1–5 and whether the session ended by plan or by clock. After ten sessions, `gcse-progress-tracker` should be able to say whether afternoon or second-of-day sessions are where accuracy drops."
findings.evidence_needed: Diurnal variation in ADHD symptoms and stimulant duration/wear-off effects on attention (ADHD-direct); prevalence of sleep problems in adolescent ADHD and effect on next-day attention (ADHD-direct).

findings.title: Frustration is handled; silent disengagement is not, and there is no way back after a break
findings.where: maths-tutor-session/SKILL.md line 74, section 'Teaching rules', 'Tone' bullet, second sentence
findings.problem: Current text: "If she's frustrated, pause the maths, be kind, suggest a break, keep it short; anything beyond normal study frustration → gently encourage talking to her parent." It triggers only on visible frustration, offers a break as a suggestion (which a 13-year-old will decline), and says nothing about how to resume. In chat the signals arrive earlier and quieter: one-word answers, 'idk', the same wrong step three times, working that stops being shown, long gaps. The 2 Sep session 3 pattern (working disappears, then questions go unfinished) is disengagement without any recorded frustration.
findings.why_it_matters: Emotional dysregulation and rapid task aversion are part of ADHD, and by the time frustration is visible in text the productive part of the session is already over. Catching it two signals earlier, giving a real choice, and returning on a guaranteed win is what keeps a wobble from becoming the end of the session and a demotion.
findings.proposal: Replace the second sentence of the Tone bullet with a separate bullet: "**Disengagement shows in text before it shows in words.** Signals: answers shrinking to one word, 'idk', the same wrong step three times, a gap of several minutes, working that was arriving and has stopped. On the second signal, stop the maths for one message: name it lightly ('that one's been a grind'), offer three choices — 5-minute break, one easier question, or stop here and log — and take whichever she picks without negotiation. After a break, come back on a question she will get, then resume; never make the return a recap or a lecture. Anything beyond normal study frustration → gently encourage talking to her parent, and put a one-line 'Note for parent' in the summary."
findings.evidence_needed: Emotional dysregulation / frustration tolerance in ADHD and the effect of choice-provision on task engagement (ADHD-direct; choice-making has behavioural-intervention evidence in ADHD classrooms).

findings.title: The skipping script is one rung; it needs a ladder, a 'which is it?' fork, and praise that carries information
findings.where: maths-tutor-session/SKILL.md line 69, section 'Teaching rules', 'The skipping habit' bullet
findings.problem: Current text: "**The skipping habit:** if she says 'skip it' or 'I can't', respond 'what's one thing you could write down?' and remind her blanks score zero but working scores method marks. Praise attempts explicitly, every time." It has worked on blanks. But it is a single move with no next step if 'one thing' does not unstick her, it treats 'I can't' (does not know where to start) and 'skip it' (does not want to) as the same, the blanks reminder repeated per question becomes nagging, and 'praise every time' makes praise non-contingent — praise that is always there stops being information about what was good.
findings.why_it_matters: Graduated prompting (least-to-most) is how you get an avoidant student moving without doing it for her, and specific contingent praise is the best-evidenced reinforcement in ADHD behavioural work; generic praise on every attempt is not. The failure mode has moved from blanks to rushing (answer-only, answer-targeting), so the script needs to reward the working, not the attempt.
findings.proposal: Replace with: "**'Skip it' / 'I can't':** first ask which it is — 'don't know where to start, or don't fancy it?' Then the ladder, one rung per message, stopping at the first that gets her moving: (1) 'what's one thing you could write down?' — the numbers from the question, the formula from the sheet, a sketch; (2) 'what does that give you?'; (3) offer two possible next steps and let her pick; (4) you do the step, she does the next one. Remind her that blanks score zero and working scores method marks once per session, not per question. Praise the specific thing, with the mark it earns ('you wrote the four terms out before collecting — that's the M mark'), not the attempt in general, and not every time."
findings.evidence_needed: Least-to-most / graduated prompting and specific contingent praise in ADHD behavioural interventions (ADHD-direct, meta-analysis of behavioural parent/teacher training); scaffolding fading (general).

findings.title: No transition scripts between blocks, and the exit-ticket rules are never told to her
findings.where: maths-tutor-session/SKILL.md lines 54-57, Shape A steps 1-4 (the blocks are listed; nothing joins them)
findings.problem: The four blocks are specified but nothing says how one becomes the next. 'Mark together' ends the starter; the teach block simply begins. The exit ticket says 'done independently' — a rule for the tutor — but she is never told 'no hints from me on these four, this is where the topic earns its 🟢', so from her side an exit ticket looks like more practice, and the 'independent' status of the evidence depends on her not asking.
findings.why_it_matters: Task switching is expensive for ADHD; an unmarked transition is where attention leaks, and an unexplained change of rules (suddenly no hints) reads as the tutor going cold. A one-line result plus a one-line frame in the same message closes one block and opens the next with nothing to fall into.
findings.proposal: Add to 'Opening and closing': "### Transitions\nEnd each block with its result and start the next with its frame, in the same message: 'Starter done: 4/5 — the A4 one comes back next time. Now 20 minutes on expected frequency. First: what does \"expected\" mean to you?' Before the exit ticket, the rules once, in her terms: 'Four questions, on your own, no hints from me, working on paper, tell me when you're done. This is where the topic earns its 🟢.' If she asks for a hint during the exit ticket, give it and mark that question as supported — it still counts as evidence, just not for secure."
findings.evidence_needed: Set-shifting / task-switching costs in ADHD and the effect of explicit transition cues (ADHD-direct or classroom guideline).

findings.title: 'No walls of text' is a tone rule, not a format rule; chat needs one ask per message
findings.where: maths-tutor-session/SKILL.md line 74, 'Tone' bullet, first sentence; and line 56 ('5–8 questions')
findings.problem: Current text: "**Tone:** warm, brief, encouraging, age-appropriate; mistakes are information; no walls of text." It says what not to do and leaves the shape of a message to the model, which under a 30-40 minute teach block will drift to multi-paragraph explanations, several questions in one message and numbered instruction lists. 'Practise: 5–8 questions' invites sending the set in one go.
findings.why_it_matters: Working-memory load is the constraint: a 13-year-old with ADHD reading a chat message holds one instruction reliably, not three. A message that ends with a single, bolded, last-line ask is the difference between her acting and her scrolling. This is also the mechanism behind finding 2 — when the ask is buried, she answers the part she noticed.
findings.proposal: Replace with: "**Tone and shape:** warm, brief, encouraging, age-appropriate; mistakes are information. **One message, one ask** — every message ends with exactly one thing for her to do, and it is the last line. One question at a time, never Q1–Q3 together. At most ~60 words of explanation before the ask, then stop and let her act; a longer explanation is two turns with a question between them. No numbered instruction lists to her. Bold the thing she must notice (the number, 'simplest form', 'blues only'), not for emphasis in general."
findings.evidence_needed: Working-memory deficits in ADHD and instruction-chunking / one-step-at-a-time guidance (ADHD-direct; classroom accommodation guidelines).

findings.title: Per-question calculator labels are noise; the exam sets the mode per paper, so set it per block
findings.where: maths-tutor-session/SKILL.md line 70, 'Every question is labelled calculator or non-calculator'
findings.problem: Current text: "**Every question is labelled calculator or non-calculator.** Half of fluency work non-calculator." Combined with the starter rule 'Mix calculator/non-calculator and say which each is', every one of the 5 starter questions, 5–8 practice questions and 4 exit-ticket questions carries a label she has to read and act on (calculator out, calculator away). That is 14–17 mode switches per session for a student whose attention is the scarce resource, and it is not what the exam does: Paper 1 is entirely non-calculator, Papers 2 and 3 entirely calculator.
findings.why_it_matters: Each label is a small attentional demand and a physical switch, and mid-block switching is exactly the thing the exam never asks of her. Setting the mode once per block mimics the paper, removes a dozen micro-decisions, and still delivers the 'half non-calculator' balance across a week.
findings.proposal: Replace with: "**Calculator mode is set per block, not per question.** Say it once at the start of the starter, the practice set and the exit ticket — 'this set is non-calculator, calculator away' — as a paper does. Switch mid-block only for a stated reason. Across a week, about half of fluency work is non-calculator; alternate the starter's mode session by session." And in Shape A step 1 delete 'Mix calculator/non-calculator and say which each is.'
